newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish banks slow to up credit rate after NBP rise.
newsitem.headline: Polish banks slow to up credit rate after NBP rise.

text.p: Large Polish commercial banks have so far refrained from increasing their credit rates after the National Bank of Poland (NBP) increased official rates as of Monday, but most said decisions would be made within weeks.
The country's largest savings bank, the state-owned PKO BP, which sets the tone for many smaller commercial banks, said that any rate rise decision would probably not be quick.

"Such a decision (whether to raise credit rates) will take a long time, it will not be quick," PKO's spokesman Janusz Ostaszewski told Reuters, adding that after the bank's board meets on Thursday more information could be available.

The central bank on Monday increased its lombard rate by two points to 27 percent and its discount rate by 2.5 points to 24.5 percent in order to cool domestic demand fuelled by fast growing credit action.
Banks said that their credit and deposit rates were more often based on market than official rates, so the NBP rate rise would not make much difference.

"Our bank scarcely uses NBP credit (the lombard rate), therefore we do not have to react immediately, but we expect a reaction... in two or three weeks," said Marek Klucinski, spokesman for Powszechny Bank Kredytowy SA (PBK SA).

Banks said the central bank's plans to start collecting deposits from the public, in order to neutralise additional government spending on flood relief and reconstruction, would probably keep banks' deposit rates from falling.
The NBP said it planned to open six- and nine-month deposits, but has not given any time schedule for the move.
